questions.prompt: What is the defining feature of an AI agent compared to a single LLM call?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The LLM's outputs control what happens next in a loop, informed by results of its own previous actions

The key difference is dynamic, LLM-driven control flow across multiple steps — not just that an LLM is involved, which is also true of a single Q&A call.
keyPoints: The key difference is dynamic, LLM-driven control flow across multiple steps — not just that an LLM is involved, which is also true of a single Q&A call.

questions.prompt: What is a real cost of using an agentic loop compared to a single LLM call?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: More LLM calls per task, more latency, less predictability, and more failure surface

Each loop iteration typically costs at least one more LLM call, and the unpredictable step count makes agents slower, costlier, and harder to test than simpler approaches.
keyPoints: Each loop iteration typically costs at least one more LLM call, and the unpredictable step count makes agents slower, costlier, and harder to test than simpler approaches.

questions.prompt: Why does having a very large number of available tools (dozens or hundreds) make tool selection harder?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: More tools competing for attention increases the odds of a wrong pick and can eat into context budget just listing them

As the number of options grows, so does the chance of confusion between similar tools, and simply listing every tool definition can consume a meaningful share of the prompt's context budget.
keyPoints: As the number of options grows, so does the chance of confusion between similar tools, and simply listing every tool definition can consume a meaningful share of the prompt's context budget.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of a purely reactive agent that decides only its next step at each point?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It may miss opportunities to parallelize independent sub-steps or notice redundant steps, since it has no explicit overall plan

Without an explicit representation of the whole task's structure, a purely reactive agent can't recognize opportunities like parallelizable sub-steps that a planning approach would catch.
keyPoints: Without an explicit representation of the whole task's structure, a purely reactive agent can't recognize opportunities like parallelizable sub-steps that a planning approach would catch.

questions.prompt: What is short-term memory in an agent, as described in this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: Short-term memory is the accumulating context within one task's loop — it exists only for the duration of that run, unlike long-term memory which is meant to persist.
keyPoints: Short-term memory is the accumulating context within one task's loop — it exists only for the duration of that run, unlike long-term memory which is meant to persist.

choices.text: Information stored permanently in an external database
The running history of thoughts, actions, and observations within a single task's execution
A summary of every past user interaction ever recorded
The model's pretraining data

questions.prompt: Why might an agent's task need to be paused and resumed across separate sessions rather than completing in one continuous run?
questions.referenceAnswer: Real tasks sometimes need to wait on external events or explicit approval, which means the run can't simply continue uninterrupted and must be able to persist and resume.
keyPoints: Real tasks sometimes need to wait on external events or explicit approval, which means the run can't simply continue uninterrupted and must be able to persist and resume.

choices.text: Agents can never take more than one step
The task might wait on a slow external process or require human approval before continuing
Pausing is never actually needed for real agent tasks
Context windows make pausing unnecessary

questions.prompt: What should a handoff between agents generally include, beyond the raw sub-task?
questions.referenceAnswer: A well-designed handoff includes the sub-task, distilled relevant context, and clear completion expectations — not just a bare task description, and not the entire raw history either.
keyPoints: A well-designed handoff includes the sub-task, distilled relevant context, and clear completion expectations — not just a bare task description, and not the entire raw history either.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the bare sub-task description
Relevant context the receiver needs, and a clear expectation of what a completed response looks like
The entire sending agent's raw internal history with no distillation
A list of every tool that exists in the whole system

questions.prompt: Why isn't checking only the final outcome sufficient to evaluate an agent?
questions.referenceAnswer: A correct-looking result can mask an inefficient, risky, or lucky process — trajectory evaluation is needed to catch that gap that outcome-only checks can't see.
keyPoints: A correct-looking result can mask an inefficient, risky, or lucky process — trajectory evaluation is needed to catch that gap that outcome-only checks can't see.

choices.text: Outcomes are never measurable for agents
An agent can reach a correct final answer through an unreliable or unsafe process that happened to work out this particular time
Final outcomes are always wrong for agents
Outcome evaluation requires no reference answer

questions.prompt: An agent repeatedly calls the same tool without finishing. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect state transitions and repeated observations. Set step, cost and retry budgets. Define termination conditions and test recovery from tool errors.
keyPoints: Inspect state transitions and repeated observations.
Set step, cost and retry budgets.
Define termination conditions and test recovery from tool errors.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Define termination conditions and test recovery from tool errors. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Define termination conditions and test recovery from tool errors.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Inspect state transitions and repeated observations. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Inspect state transitions and repeated observations.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
